chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Firecraft → Bow Drill Friction Fire
chunks.text:
Difficulty:

Advanced

A bow drill creates heat through friction until a glowing ember forms.

It is a valuable training skill but should not be considered the primary emergency ignition method for an untrained person.

Fireboard

Creates friction dust.

Spindle

Rotates against the fireboard.

Bow

Provides continuous rotation.

Handhold

Applies pressure while reducing top friction.

Procedure

Prepare the fireboard socket.

Create a notch for collecting hot dust.

Assemble the spindle and bow.

Drill with steady pressure.

Build enough heat to create an ember.

Transfer ember into prepared tinder.

Add airflow until flame develops.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Firecraft → Building A Basic Survival Fire
chunks.text:
Overview

Create a dependable fire using simple materials.

Step 1 --- Select A Safe Fire Location

Choose:

stable ground;

an area clear of dry vegetation;

protection from strong wind;

sufficient space above the fire.

Prepare the area:

Clear flammable material around the fire location.

Keep fuel organized before ignition.

Keep water or another extinguishing method available when possible.

Never leave a fire unattended.

Use existing fire rings or designated fire areas when available. Safe campfire guidance emphasizes clearing combustible material, controlling fire size, monitoring the fire, and fully extinguishing before leaving.

Step 2 --- Prepare Fuel Before Lighting

Collect:

Tinder

Enough for the first flame.

Kindling

Several handfuls of progressively larger sticks.

Fuel Wood

Enough to maintain the fire.

A common mistake is lighting the fire before collecting enough material.

Prepare first.

Ignite second.

Teepee Fire

Best for:

fast ignition;

beginners;

quick heating.

Construction:

Place tinder in the center.

Lean small sticks around the tinder.

Leave openings for airflow.

Increase stick size as the flame grows.

Lean-To Fire

Best for:

wind protection;

protected ignition.

Construction:

Place a larger support stick.

Lean smaller sticks against it.

Place tinder underneath.

Add larger fuel gradually.

Log Cabin Fire

Best for:

stable heat;

longer burning;

cooking.

Construction:

Place larger pieces as a base.

Stack smaller pieces across them.

Leave airflow gaps.

Build tinder inside.

Step 4 --- Ignite And Build The Fire

The fire grows through stages:

TINDER

↓

SMALL FLAME

↓

KINDLING

↓

FUEL WOOD

Once the tinder catches:

Protect the flame from wind.

Add small kindling.

Allow heat to build.

Add larger wood gradually.

Do not overload a small flame.

Overview

A fire is finished only when it is cold.

Procedure:

Stop adding fuel.

Add water.

Stir ashes and coals.

Add more water.

Check for remaining heat.

If it is not cool to the touch, it is not fully extinguished.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Firecraft → Fire As A Signal
chunks.text:
Overview

Fire may improve visibility during rescue situations.

Possible methods:

visible flame at night;

smoke during daylight when appropriate;

reflective signaling combined with other methods.

Always balance signaling with fire safety and environmental conditions.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Firecraft → Fire In Wet Conditions
chunks.text:
Overview

Wet environments require better preparation.

The goal is not finding dry-looking wood.

The goal is finding usable dry material.

Standing Dead Wood

Dead standing branches often contain drier internal wood.

Protected Material

Search:

under larger branches;

inside dead wood;

under natural cover.

Split Wood

Outer surfaces may be wet.

The interior may remain dry.

Method:

Method:

Split larger wood.

Remove wet outer layers.

Use dry inner material.

Step 1

Create a dry platform.

Use:

bark;

small sticks;

dry wood.

Step 2

Create Fine Tinder

Smaller material ignites more easily.

Step 3

Build Gradually

Use:

Tinder

↓

Fine Kindling

↓

Small Wood

↓

Large Fuel

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Firecraft → Fire With A Ferrocerium Rod
chunks.text:
Overview

Create ignition sparks without relying on fuel-based lighters.

A ferrocerium rod produces hot sparks, but success depends mainly on preparation:

suitable tinder;

correct technique;

dry combustible material.

Step 1 --- Prepare Tinder

Prepare the catching material before striking.

Examples:

fine wood shavings;

dry bark fibers;

prepared fire starter.

Step 2 --- Position The Rod

Place sparks directly into the tinder.

Distance matters.

Closer sparks transfer more heat.

Step 3 --- Strike

Methods:

Pull Method

Hold the striker steady and pull the rod backward.

Advantages:

better control;

less disturbance to tinder.

Push Method

Hold the rod steady and push the striker forward.

Step 4 --- Build The Flame

After ignition:

Add fine material.

Protect airflow.

Increase fuel size gradually.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Firecraft → Using Fire For Water And Cooking
chunks.text:
Overview

Fire can support:

boiling water;

cooking food;

warming equipment.

For water purification:

For water purification:

Collect water.

Remove visible particles when possible.

Heat water to a rolling boil.

Follow current public-health guidance for boiling time and elevation.

Boiling is effective against many biological hazards but does not remove chemical contamination.

Overview

Maintain mobility.

Foot injuries can end a wilderness trip.

Prevention

Use:

proper footwear;

dry socks;

reduced friction.

Treatment

Protect intact blisters.

For open blisters:

Clean.

Cover.

Reduce friction.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter First Aidcraft → Building A Survival First-Aid Kit

chunks.text:
Overview

Limit tissue damage and protect the wound.

Thermal

Fire, hot liquids, hot objects.

Chemical

Corrosive substances.

Electrical

Electrical energy injuries.

Step 1

Remove from heat source.

Step 2

Cool the burn with clean cool water when available.

Step 3

Remove tight items before swelling increases.

Step 4

Cover with clean non-stick material.

Stabilize Injuries, Prevent Deterioration, And Keep A Person Alive Until Help Arrives

Wilderness first aid is different from normal first aid.

The main goal is not complete treatment.

The goal is:

keep the person alive;

prevent the injury from becoming worse;

maintain basic function;

prepare for evacuation.

A survival medical system is:

ASSESS

-

CONTROL LIFE THREATS

-

PROTECT

-

STABILIZE

-

EVACUATE

The First Aid Priority System

Treat problems in order of urgency.

1. Safety

Before helping:

Check:

environment;

hazards;

weather;

ongoing danger.

A rescuer who becomes injured creates a second emergency.

2. Response

Check:

Is the person conscious?

Can they communicate?

Are they breathing normally?

Can they communicate?

3. Life-Threatening Bleeding

Severe bleeding can become fatal quickly.

Control major bleeding immediately.

4. Airway And Breathing

Check for:

blocked airway;

breathing difficulty;

severe respiratory problems.

5. Shock And Environmental Injury

Protect against:

heat loss;

overheating;

dehydration;

worsening injury.

Overview

Reduce movement and prevent further damage.

Signs

Possible signs:

severe pain;

swelling;

deformity;

loss of function.

Step 1

Keep the injured area still.

Step 2

Support with padding or splint.

Step 3

Secure above and below the injury.

Step 4

Check circulation.

Cause

Heat stress combined with fluid and electrolyte loss.

Signs

Possible signs:

heavy sweating;

weakness;

dizziness;

headache;

nausea.

Step 1

Move to a cooler location.

Step 2

Stop activity.

Step 3

Cool the body.

Methods:

shade;

wet cloth;

airflow.

Step 4

Replace fluids if the person is alert and able to drink.

Overview

Recognize a medical emergency.

Heat stroke requires rapid cooling and urgent medical care. Current wilderness medicine guidance emphasizes immediate cooling when heat stroke is suspected.

Signs

Possible signs:

confusion;

collapse;

altered behavior;

seizure;

severe overheating.

Step 1

Move away from heat.

Step 2

Begin rapid cooling.

Begin rapid cooling.

Preferred methods when available:

cold-water immersion;

aggressive cooling with water and airflow.

Step 3

Arrange emergency evacuation.

Cause

The body loses heat faster than it can replace it.

Signs

Early:

shivering;

fatigue;

poor coordination.

Advanced:

confusion;

slurred speech;

reduced consciousness.

Step 1

Move into shelter.

Step 2

Remove wet clothing.

Step 3

Add insulation.

Step 4

Protect from ground contact.

Step 5

Warm gradually.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter First Aidcraft → Severe Bleeding Control
chunks.text:
Overview

Stop life-threatening blood loss.

Modern first-aid guidance emphasizes rapid control of severe bleeding using direct pressure and appropriate use of tourniquets for life-threatening limb bleeding.

Step 1 --- Apply Direct Pressure

Use:

gauze;

dressing;

clean cloth.

Press firmly.

Maintain pressure.

Step 2 --- Pack Deep Wounds

For appropriate deep wounds:

Place dressing material into the wound.

Fill the space.

Maintain firm pressure.

Step 3 --- Apply Pressure Bandage

Secure the dressing while maintaining pressure.

Step 4 --- Tourniquet Use

Use for:

severe bleeding from an arm or leg;

bleeding that cannot be controlled by direct pressure.

Tourniquet Placement

Place:

above the wound;

between wound and body;

away from joints.

Application

Tighten until severe bleeding stops.

Record application time.

Leave in place until medical professionals take over.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter First Aidcraft → Wound Cleaning And Care
chunks.text:
Overview

Reduce infection risk.

Step 1

Control bleeding.

Step 2

Flush contamination using clean water when available.

Step 3

Cover with clean dressing.

Step 4

Monitor.

Watch for:

increasing redness;

swelling;

worsening pain;

drainage;

fever.

Method 1 --- Roasting

Best for:

fish;

meat pieces.

Procedure:

Prepare food.

Place near controlled heat.

Rotate regularly.

Cook completely.

Method 2 --- Boiling

Best for:

meat;

plants;

soups.

Procedure:

Add food and water.

Heat thoroughly.

Maintain cooking temperature.

Method 3 --- Coal Cooking

Provides:

stable heat;

better temperature control.

Overview

Use calories efficiently and reduce unnecessary energy loss.

Energy Loss Increases With:

cold exposure;

heat exposure;

heavy movement;

carrying loads;

dehydration;

stress.

Reduce Unnecessary Movement

Travel with a purpose.

Avoid wasting energy searching without a plan.

Maintain Shelter

A protected body uses less energy maintaining temperature.

Stay Hydrated

Dehydration reduces physical and mental performance.

Rest Strategically

Recover before exhaustion.

Overview

Prepare fish safely for cooking.

Step 1

Secure the fish.

Step 2

Remove internal organs.

Step 3

Clean using safe water when available.

Step 4

Cook thoroughly.

Food safety guidance recommends cooking seafood thoroughly and avoiding undercooked animal products.

Overview

Extend food usefulness.

Drying

Removes moisture.

Smoking

Uses smoke exposure for preservation and flavor.

Salting

Reduces available moisture.

Preservation Principle

Food preservation reduces spoilage by controlling:

moisture;

temperature;

contamination.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Foodcraft → Hunting And Small Game

chunks.text:
Overview

Create renewable food sources during extended situations.

Gardening is a long-term strategy.

It requires:

time;

water;

sunlight;

suitable soil.

Fast Crops

Provide quicker harvest.

Calorie Crops

Provide energy.

Examples:

potatoes;

grains where suitable.

Protein Crops

Examples:

beans;

peas.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Foodcraft → Survival Food Decision Making
chunks.text:
Overview

Before searching for food, ask:

1. How Long Will The Emergency Last?

Short emergency:

Use carried food.

Long emergency:

Develop food sources.

2. Is The Food Worth The Energy Cost?

A dangerous search may provide fewer calories than it consumes.

3. Is Identification Certain?

Unknown food creates unnecessary risk.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Foodcraft → Using Stored Survival Food
Chapter Foodcraft → Wild Game Food Safety
chunks.text:
Overview

Reduce foodborne illness risk.

Handling Principles

Keep:

meat clean;

tools clean;

raw meat separated from cooked food.

Cook Thoroughly

Wild game can contain parasites and pathogens.

Do not rely only on:

appearance;

smell;

texture.

Wild game safety guidance emphasizes hygienic handling and thorough cooking.

Overview

A rescue-friendly location should have:

Visibility

Make yourself easier to see.

Signals

Repeat signals.

Organization

Keep:

shelter;

water;

fire;

medical supplies

together.

Overview

Help rescuers locate you.

Sound Signals

A whistle is effective because it carries farther than shouting.

Use repeated patterns.

Visual Signals

Use:

bright clothing;

emergency blanket;

tarp;

signal mirror.

Create contrast against the environment.

Light Signals

Use:

flashlight;

headlamp;

reflective surfaces.

Electronic Signals

Devices include:

Gps Messenger

Can send:

location;

messages;

emergency alerts.

Personal Locator Beacon (Plb)

Designed for emergency distress signaling through satellite systems.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Navigationcraft → Navigation In Different Environments

chunks.text:
Overview

Night increases difficulty.

Challenges:

Challenges:

reduced visibility;

distance errors;

terrain hazards.

Slow Down

Move carefully.

Use Compass

Natural direction clues become weaker.

Protect Night Vision

Avoid unnecessary bright light.

Overview

Understand the landscape before moving.

A topographic map represents the three-dimensional landscape on a two-dimensional surface.

Scale

Shows distance relationship between map and ground.

Legend

Explains symbols.

Includes:

trails;

roads;

water;

landmarks.

Contour Lines

Show elevation changes.

Close Lines

Steep terrain.

Wide Lines

Gentle slopes.

V-Shaped Lines

Usually indicate valleys or drainage.

Circular Lines

Usually indicate hills or elevated terrain.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Navigationcraft → Survival Decision Making When Lost

chunks.text:
Overview

Determine a direction of travel.

Step 1

Identify destination.

Example:

mountain;

trail junction;

landmark.

Step 2

Point direction arrow toward destination.

Step 3

Rotate compass housing until north aligns.

Step 4

Read the bearing.

Following A Bearing

Hold compass level.

Align direction.

Select a visible landmark ahead.

Travel toward that landmark.

Repeat.

Avoid staring only at the compass while moving.

Maintain terrain awareness.

Overview

Navigate by understanding the shape of the land.

Ridge

High narrow land formation.

Valley

Low area between higher terrain.

Saddle

Lower area between two high points.

Peak

Highest point in an area.

Drainage

Area where water flows downhill.

Terrain Association Method

Identify terrain around you.

Compare it with the map.

Confirm location.

Choose route.

Continue checking.

Good navigation is continuous, not a single decision.

Overview

Maintain direction when landmarks are limited.

Magnetic Needle

Points toward magnetic north.

Direction Arrow

Shows intended travel direction.

Rotating Housing

Used for bearings.

Baseplate

Used with maps.

Magnetic Declination

Magnetic north and true north are different.

The difference is called magnetic declination.

Set your compass for the area you are traveling before relying on precise bearings.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Navigationcraft → Using Stars For Direction
chunks.text:
Northern Hemisphere --- Polaris

Polaris is located close to true north.

Finding Polaris

Find the Big Dipper.

Locate the two outer stars of the bowl.

Extend an imaginary line through them.

Continue about five times their distance.

Locate Polaris.

The direction toward Polaris is approximately north.

Southern Hemisphere

Polaris is not visible.

Southern navigation requires different star patterns, including use of the Southern Cross.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Navigationcraft → Using The Sun For Direction
chunks.text:
Overview

Provide a general direction reference.

Basic Principle

The sun generally:

rises in the east;

sets in the west.

The exact position changes with season and location.

Materials

straight stick;

open ground;

sunlight.

Procedure

Place stick vertically.

Mark the shadow tip.

Wait approximately 15--20 minutes.

Mark the new shadow tip.

Draw a line between marks.

The first mark is approximately west.

The second mark is approximately east.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Navigationcraft → Using Waterways For Navigation

chunks.text:
Overview

Create rapid weather protection.

A tarp is one of the most efficient emergency shelter tools because it is:

lightweight;

waterproof;

reusable;

fast to deploy.

Equipment

tarp;

cord;

anchors or stakes.

Best For

rain;

wind;

general protection.

Step 1

Find secure anchor points.

Step 2

Create a ridgeline.

Step 3

Place tarp over the line.

Step 4

Secure corners.

Step 5

Adjust height.

Lower:

in strong wind;

in cold conditions.

Raise:

in warm conditions;

when ventilation is needed.

Best For

quick shelter;

fire-side protection when conditions allow.

Construction

Attach one side higher.

Angle tarp downward.

Secure lower edge.

Adjust for wind direction.

Overview

Create an insulated emergency shelter in woodland environments.

A debris hut works by trapping air inside layers of dry insulating material.

Materials

ridgepole;

branches;

leaves;

grass;

needles.

Step 1

Build a strong ridgepole.

Step 2

Create a supporting frame.

Step 3

Add cross branches.

Step 4

Cover with thick insulation.

Use:

dry leaves;

grass;

needles.

Step 5

Create an insulated sleeping area.

The body should not contact cold ground.

Step 6

Control the entrance.

Reduce unnecessary openings while maintaining airflow.

Overview

Prevent heat transfer into the ground.

Materials

Use:

sleeping pad;

backpack;

clothing;

dry leaves;

grass;

pine needles;

natural vegetation.

Method

Create a thick layer between:

BODY

and

GROUND

GROUND

Field Principle

The shelter does not create heat.

Your body creates heat.

The shelter reduces heat loss.

Overview

Improve a basic shelter by adding:

More Insulation

Increase material thickness.

Better Ground Protection

Improve sleeping insulation.

Wind Blocking

Close exposed sides.

Ventilation

Maintain airflow, especially when using any heat source.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Sheltercraft → Selecting A Shelter Location

chunks.text:
Overview

A survival shelter should have clear zones.

Sleeping Zone

Purpose:

rest;

recovery;

temperature control.

Fire Zone

Purpose:

warmth;

cooking.

Maintain safe fire control.

Equipment Zone

Protect:

clothing;

tools;

food.

Water Zone

Separate:

untreated water;

drinking water.

Overview

Use snow as an insulating material.

Snow contains trapped air, which helps reduce heat loss.

Snow Trench

A trench covered with insulating material.

Snow Cave

A shelter excavated into suitable snow.

Snow Shelter Safety

A snow shelter requires:

adequate ventilation;

stable construction;

regular checking of openings.

adequate ventilation;

stable construction;

Never use combustion devices in enclosed snow shelters without proper ventilation.

Carbon monoxide can build up without warning. Snow shelter guidance from the National Park Service emphasizes ventilation and carbon monoxide prevention.

Overview

The body loses heat through several processes.

Conduction

Heat moves from your body into colder surfaces.

Example:

Sleeping directly on cold ground.

Solution:

Create insulation underneath your body.

Convection

Moving air removes heat.

Example:

Cold wind passing over exposed skin.

Solution:

Block wind.

Evaporation

Water leaving the body removes heat.

Example:

Wet clothing in cold conditions.

Solution:

Keep clothing dry.

Radiation

The body naturally releases heat into the environment.

Solution:

Add insulation and protection.

Shelter Priority

In cold environments:

GROUND INSULATION

is one of the highest priorities.

A shelter with a good roof but poor ground insulation can still allow significant heat loss.

Overview

Kill disease-causing microorganisms.

Boiling is one of the most reliable wilderness water treatment methods.

Step 1

Collect water.

Step 2

Remove visible sediment.

Allow settling or filter through clean material.

Step 3

Bring water to a rolling boil.

Step 4

Maintain boiling time.

General guidance:

1 minute at normal elevations;

3 minutes above approximately 6,500 feet (2,000 meters).

Step 5

Cool and store.

Use a clean covered container.

Important Limitation

Boiling does not remove:

fuel;

toxic chemicals;

heavy metals;

radioactive contamination.

Use another source if chemical contamination is suspected.

Overview

Capture available water efficiently.

Method 1 --- Container Collection

Best method.

Use:

bottles;

pots;

water bags;

clean containers.

Procedure:

Select the cleanest available source.

Fill container.

Protect opening from dirt.

Store safely.

Method 2 --- Rainwater Collection

Materials:

tarp;

rainfly;

clean container.

Procedure:

Create a clean collection surface.

Direct water toward a low point.

Collect in container.

Cover after collection.

Method 3 --- Snow And Ice

Snow can provide water but contains trapped air.

Procedure:

Collect clean snow.

Melt gradually.

Add a small amount of liquid water first if available.

Treat before drinking when required.

Find, Collect, Purify, And Manage Water

Water is one of the most important survival resources.

The body requires water for:

temperature regulation;

circulation;

physical performance;

mental function;

normal body processes.

A survival water system has four stages:

FIND water

COLLECT water

TREAT water

STORE water

The objective is not simply finding water.

The objective is obtaining water that is safe to drink.

The Water Survival Principle

Natural water may contain:

bacteria;

viruses;

parasites;

sediment;

chemical contamination.

Clear water is not automatically safe.

Water treatment methods solve different problems:

Filtration

Removes particles and some organisms depending on filter design.

Disinfection

Kills or inactivates many microorganisms.

Boiling

Kills disease-causing organisms through heat.

No treatment method makes chemically contaminated water safe. Water containing fuel, toxic chemicals, or radioactive materials requires a different source.

chunks.sectionPath: Chapter Watercraft → Finding Water By Environment

chunks.text:
Overview

Use sunlight to reduce microorganisms.

Basic method:

Fill clear plastic bottles with clear water.

Place in strong sunlight.

Allow sufficient exposure time.

Use afterward.

Solar disinfection is limited by:

cloudy water;

weak sunlight;

contamination type.

It does not remove chemicals.

Overview

Collect condensed moisture.

A solar still is an emergency backup method.

It usually produces small amounts of water and should not be considered a primary survival water source.

Basic Design

Materials:

plastic sheet;

container;

digging tool.

Procedure:

Dig a hole.

Place container in the center.

Cover with plastic.

Seal edges.

Place a small weight above the container.

Condensation collects and drips downward.

Overview

Use ultraviolet light to inactivate microorganisms.

Procedure

Start with clear water.

Remove cloudiness if needed.

Use the UV device according to instructions.

Store treated water safely.

UV treatment works poorly in cloudy water because particles can block light exposure.

Overview

Finding water is only part of survival.

Protect your supply.

Reduce Water Loss

Methods:

rest during extreme heat;

use shade;

protect skin from sun;

avoid unnecessary exertion.

Water Management Priority

Protect yourself from heat.

Find water early.

Collect enough supply.

Treat before drinking.

Store safely.

Conserve continuously.

Overview

Improve water quality by removing particles and some microorganisms.

Portable filters vary widely.

Always know:

what organisms the filter removes;

filter limitations;

replacement requirements.

CDC notes that many portable filters remove parasites but may not remove viruses or all bacteria. Follow manufacturer instructions and use additional treatment when required.

Step 1

Allow muddy water to settle.

Step 2

Remove visible particles.

Use:

cloth;

clean filter material.

Step 3

Use a proper water filter.

Step 4

Disinfect if required.

Overview

Protect collected water.

Use:

clean containers;

sealed bottles;

covered storage.

Separate:

Untreated Water

Potentially contaminated.

Treated Water

Ready for drinking.

Avoid mixing the two.
